_readme: The agreed status vocabulary, and a table of cases both implementations
of it must answer identically. REQ-QAC-047.
There are two implementations of dataset status in this repo and there
have to be: the dashboard computes it in the browser, and the GitHub
Issues ticketing automation computes it in a GitHub Action with no JS
runtime (qa_tools/common/dataset_status.py's own docstring explains the
split). They drifted once already - plans/qa-pipeline.md item 74 - and
the drift rendered a check with 14 real violations GREEN.
This file is owned by NEITHER of them. It is read by tests/
test_status_parity.py and by tests-js/status-parity.test.js, which run
every case below through their own side and compare. Neither suite can
quietly reinterpret a case, because neither writes it.
WHAT THIS COVERS THAT THE BROWSER CHECK DOES NOT. tests/
test_dashboard_e2e.py's TestStatusMatchesEachToolsOwnVerdict already
drives the real built dashboard over every committed result and
compares ~30k rendered statuses against the verdicts the real tools
recorded. That covers inputs nobody anticipated. It can only ever cover
statuses that APPEAR IN THE HISTORY, and the whole reason this file
exists is a status with no history at all yet: per-check nodata. A
verification that only sees what has already happened cannot catch a
value that has not happened. Neither half covers the other's gap.
ADDING A STATUS. Add it to `vocabulary` and add at least one case. Both
suites then fail until both implementations recognise it, which is the
point - a status either side does not know about must never be read as
evidence of health.

_why: Statuses a rollup can compare. The numbers ARE the rule: worst-of is
a reduce seeded at green, so nodata sits below green where it can
only ever lose. That is deliberate - 'nothing to show yet' must not
outrank a real green, and must not masquerade as the worst outcome
either.
Recognition is scoped to WHERE a status was read from, which is a
distinction the first draft of this table missed and the cases
caught. `exhausted` is a property of a dataset's SCHEDULE. A check
result carrying it means something upstream wrote a dataset-level
status onto a check, and a vocabulary flat enough to accept it
everywhere would render that bug rather than report it.
So a check may carry only the ordered statuses; a dataset tile may
carry those plus the unordered ones.
Recognised, but deliberately OUTSIDE the ordering, so a rollup
cannot absorb them. A caller that needs one surfaces it alongside
the rolled-up status, never through it.
An implementation asked to order one of these must fail rather than
return a number, because the only honest answers are 'throw' and
'green', and green is how item 74 happened.
unordered.exhausted: The dataset's authored delivery dates have run out relative to the selected as-of date (REQ-PIPE-053). Not red: a supplier's clean dataset reading red because WE forgot to type next year's dates is an attribution error. Not nodata: nodata is filtered before every rollup, so it would vanish above the tile.
unordered.inactive: No automated quality rule is defined for this column at all - neither the ODCS contract nor the Soda/dbt check files name one (post-build-review #4). Not green: green is a verdict, and a column nobody checks has not passed anything - it was the honest label being four clicks deep that made an unchecked column read as a healthy one everywhere above the check panel. Not amber or red either: nothing is failing and nobody is being asked to act on the DATA. It is INACTIVE, which is a state a reader already has a vocabulary for, and which cannot be mistaken for a verdict.

check_cases.why: The real tool already decided. Its verdict is the authority; threshold math is only ever a fallback.
Same rule in the other direction - a recorded red is not second-guessed against thresholds that would have said green.

THE BUG THIS REQUIREMENT EXISTS FOR. Python had no nodata in its ordering at all, so a recorded nodata failed the recognised-status test, fell through to threshold arithmetic, and returned green. The dashboard returned nodata for the same input.
The fallback is legitimate and must stay - not every rule fits a warn/fail pair.

item 74's original bug. The ODCS rowCount rule is a two-sided mustBeBetween, so both single-sided bounds are legitimately null. Reading null as 0 turned a real row count of 1939 into red on every run of all 7 datasets while the tools themselves all said pass.

THE DEFECT BEHIND THE BUG, and worse than it. An unrecognised status read GREEN in BOTH implementations by two different routes: Python silently fell through to threshold arithmetic, and the dashboard passed the string straight out to a rollup that could not order it and kept its green seed. Both convert 'I do not know what this is' into 'this is fine'.

Stated separately because it is the criterion, not a duplicate: the failure must not depend on what the thresholds would have said. Here they would have said red, and the previous behaviour still managed to return red for the wrong reason - having discarded the recorded value entirely.

Absent and empty are the same thing - no verdict was recorded - and neither is an unknown verdict. Kept as a case because the distinction is exactly one character of implementation apart from the fatal case above.

exhausted is a property of a dataset's schedule, not of a check result. A check claiming it means something upstream wrote a dataset-level status onto a check, which is a bug worth hearing about rather than rendering. This case is what forced recognition to be scoped by level rather than flat - see vocabulary.by_level.
The placeholder is synthesised by pipeline/build_*_dashboard_data.py, not produced by any tool, so it states its own status. It used to state green.

rollup_cases.why: The whole rule, in one case.

A reduce seeded at green. Recorded rather than assumed because it is how a table whose checks have ALL been retired renders green by vacuum in both implementations - reachable, and closed by a different gate (a zero-active-checks CI check), not here.
nodata must never win against a real status. Five green and one nodata is green.

Recorded as it really is, not as it should be. A reduce seeded at green with nodata below it means a rollup containing NOTHING BUT nodata still returns green - so a column whose only check has no data reads healthy. Both sides do this, identically, which is why it is a parity case and not a parity bug. It is a REAL false green and it is closed elsewhere: this requirement's own decision is that a structural fix elsewhere (sprint 17's red-for-unrun) is not a reason to leave the old path untested, and changing the seed here would be a behaviour change across every rollup in the dashboard on a requirement scoped to parity. Pinned so the fix is a deliberate edit to this line rather than a silent drift.
TS-19. The mechanism written to prevent a false green produces one the moment nodata becomes partial - which is why the path is tested even though red-for-unrun is intended to make it unreachable.

The criterion is 'SHALL NOT return green', and throwing is the only other honest answer. Silently dropping it returns green; ordering it invents a ranking nobody agreed. This is the case that catches an exhausted dataset leaking into a rollup it was supposed to be surfaced beside.
Separately from the check-level guard, because a rollup can be handed statuses from somewhere that never went through a check at all.

Stated because the previous case would also pass an implementation that only failed when the answer WOULD have been green. The failure is about not being able to order it, not about the result being flattering.

post-build-review #4. `inactive` is recognised and deliberately outside the ordering, so worst_of must refuse it rather than rank it. Ranking it low makes it lose every rollup and vanish; ranking it high makes an unasked question outrank a real failure. The filtering behaviour lives in dataset_rollup_cases below, which is where a caller that must handle it does so explicitly.
Same rule with a real verdict present - dropping it silently is how item 74 happened.

retired_cases.why: A retired check must never turn a dataset red. Both sides agree on the rule; they express it differently, which is what the next case is about.
Retirement is a hand-authored declaration, never inferred from absence.
Same, for a check whose definition predates the field.

A REAL PARITY GAP, found writing this table. The dashboard tests `retired_as_of != null`, so an empty string read as RETIRED; Python tests truthiness, so the same check read as ACTIVE. One character of difference, opposite answers, and the dashboard's reading is the dangerous one - it drops a live check from the rollup. Empty means nobody wrote a date, so the check is active.

_why: worst_of() orders. THIS rolls a whole column or dataset up, which
means first deciding what to do with the statuses that carry no
verdict at all. Both sides need it and only the dashboard had it:
Python's dataset_status() called worst_of() directly, so the first
check carrying `inactive` would have thrown inside the GitHub Issues
automation (post-build-review #4).
The rule, in one sentence: a status carrying no verdict never
competes with one that does, and never disappears either.

cases.why: An unchecked column must not drag a dataset down - nothing is failing.
The other direction. A real passing check is a verdict; an inactive one is the absence of a question, and must not outrank it.

The case the finding is actually about: a table-scope placeholder was rolling a whole Table-level section to GREEN on its own, because green was the placeholder's recorded status and nothing above the check panel distinguished 'no rule' from 'rule passed'.
Same rule, not an artefact of there being one.
Both are quiet and they say different things. 'Nobody defined a rule' is a standing fact somebody can act on; 'no run within tolerance as of this date' is temporal and may resolve itself tomorrow.

An ended schedule is the reason nothing is happening at all, so it stays the headline. Unchanged behaviour, recorded because adding a third quiet state is exactly when an existing precedence quietly changes.
Unchanged, and pinned here too: a reduce seeded at green. See nodata-alone-is-green-and-that-is-a-known-false-green for the limitation this shares and post-build-review #45 for who owns it.
Adding a third quiet state must not disturb the existing two. Recorded because precedence lists are exactly where that happens.
